utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This morning -- I take it we are starting with Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. That's correct. I'm calling the witness, defendant, my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He may take the witness stand and make the solemn declaration. Yes. Please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Prior to beginning, Your Honours, allow me to address the Court with the issue regarding the time consumption or time limitations of the examination-in-chief of Dr. Simic. My understanding is that the list that the Defence provided to the Trial Chamber according to the instructions is related to the order of the Trial Chamber. But also my understanding is that this particular case with the testimony of the defendant will not affect the time limits imposed by the Trial Chamber with regard to the other witnesses. So I just want to clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The defendant will be given sufficient time to present his case. So you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours, for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Simic. Can you hear me? Can you hear the interpretation? Did you hear the interpretation of what was just discussed with the Trial Chamber? Is everything all right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before we start, could you please be so kind as to explain briefly to the Trial Chamber why you decided to testify, why you decided to give evidence, since you are aware of the fact that this is not compulsory in such proceedings, that the Rules do not make this compulsory.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I wanted my own views to be heard in these proceedings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, 1960, Kruskovo Polje, municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Kruskovo Polje is part of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is 7 kilometres away from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which direction? North? South? East? West?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: South, towards Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, your parents still live in Kruskovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your father, what is his occupation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He used to be a financial expert. Now he is a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, since we speak the same language, when I finish putting my question, could you pause 45 seconds so that the interpreters could finish doing their work so that we could have an accurate transcript. So your father was born, I assume, also in Kruskovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Also in Kruskovo Polje -- my paternal grandfather, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in this case your great-grandfather?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Also in Kruskovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So several generations of your family have already been living in Samac, or rather, in that area?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. At least for 400 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your mother, Dr. Simic? What is her occupation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: She is a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was she born?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The village Obednik [phoen], municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that her ancestors also hailed from that area.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I have one brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was he born?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was he also born in Kruskovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is his occupation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He has an MS in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What does he do now?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He is Secretary for Economic Affairs in the municipal assembly. He was a member of the mayor's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that he has a family as well?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're married?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long have you been married?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What does your wife do? What is her occupation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: She has a degree from the higher school of social sciences, and right now she is working in a pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is she also studying something from the field of pharmacy?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. She is studying in order to obtain a degree in pharmacy at the university in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How many children do you have, you and your wife?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My wife bore four children, four of our children; three are alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding that you lost one child?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am not going to go into the details. Of course this is your private affair. How old was your child when it died?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Five months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for your other children, how many daughters, sons do you have? Of what ages are they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I have a 17-year-old son and I have two daughters. One is 14 and the other one is 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you complete elementary school?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about secondary school?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In relation to Samac, where is Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: 18 kilometres to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is Gradacac now in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What degree do you have from university?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I completed medical school in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that after obtaining the degree in medicine, you people who are involved in this line of work specialise. What was your specialist training? What did you do in the field of medicine?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did several residencies, smaller and bigger ones. In 1987, I was trained for treating chronic alcoholics in Jagomir near Sarajevo. Then in 1990, I was trained as a resident for six months in Tuzla in order to work on chemodialysis. Then in 1991, I obtained a residency in the field of internal medicine. I did this pre-clinical training in 1990, and in 1991 in Doboj and Tuzla; however, due to the war operations, in 1994 I changed my residency to epidemiology, and in 1996 I got my degree as a specialist in Banja Luka. Then, I took a post-graduate course in Banja Luka. I completed my first year of post-graduate studies. And due to what happened then, I did not continue my post-graduate studies. I can say that I am the first physician in Samac who started with chemodialysis who opened this process and introduced this at the Samac Medical Centre for Chemodialysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned epidemiology as your specialist training, and this was practically during the time of war?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for you to opt for that field of medicine?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because I could deal with that theoretically to a large extent and I didn't have to get that much practical training, because I didn't have enough time to spend at clinical facilities. That meant that I would have to leave town for several years and so on to go to a larger medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This field of medicine, epidemiology, was it of relevance to the town, for example, during the war operations, in terms of providing better healthcare to the population? Please just answer -- just wait --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It can be said that it is logical for that to be the most important field of medicine in a time of war, in addition to war surgery, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned this centre for dialysis at the medical centre in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think I have a problem again. Two days in a row, I don't have the button correctly adjusted. Dr. Simic, I -- being that I'm not an expert medical person, I wonder whether you could tell me exactly what epidemiology is and why it would be important in a wartime armed conflict-type of situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Epidemiology is a science that previously dealt only with the spread of contagious diseases. However, today it also has to deal with the spread of non-contagious diseases. So nutrition is a very important field, generally speaking. However, in a situation of war, due to poor hygiene, contagious diseases are on the rise. And therefore, it is the task of epidemiologists to propose measures that curb the degree and control the spread of contagious diseases, because then there is no electricity, there is no water, there is poor nutrition, and so on and so forth, poor hygiene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this centre for dialysis at the medical centre in Samac. Please tell us now briefly, why was it necessary to establish the centre for dialysis and what is -- what is it so particular about that region where you lived?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In the valley of Sava -- or rather, the Sava Valley all the way down to the Black Sea, that area is known for endemic kidney diseases, nephropathy, which leads to deterioration of kidneys. And since this is an endemic area, and we are within that area, we had to open a centre for dialysis in order to treat chronic kidney patients. Their natural kidneys stopped functioning and then they have to use artificial ones. It enables them to extend their life for some ten years. And after chemodialysis becomes impossible, then they can proceed to transplantation of kidneys providing that that surgery is successful, they continue with a normal life. And if it fails, then they have to go back to dialysis. So this is a method that cleans the blood. It's called an artificial kidney.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, during war operations in Samac, did this centre continue to operate?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did throughout the war, and it provided services to all patients with kidney problems residing in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "all patients residing in Samac," do you mean regardless of their ethnic or religious background?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, when did you complete your military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In which branch of service did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And upon completing your military service, you became a member of the reserve forces, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what reserve forces were you a member of.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Medical corps within the Territorial Defence in Samac municipality. I think that I was listed there as head of the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you from time to time also perform certain -- did you participate in certain military training, as was mandated by the law?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were regular trainings, and they existed within the framework of National Defence and Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the unit that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Ivo Dragicevic was the commander. He was the Chief of Staff of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Until the -- until he was forcibly removed, until the 16th of April, 1992. He's Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you mean by "forcible removal." Who removed him forcibly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He was removed by the coalition of the HDZ and SDA. The then-president or mayor of municipality issued an order that he be removed, and that was done without the consent of Serb representatives, assemblymen, and other official organs of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since something was not recorded in the transcript -- you mentioned the name of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Just a kind of intervention and suggestion to the Translation Unit. If we are speaking of the chairman of the municipal assembly, that sense is rather different than the term "mayor" -- "mayor of municipality," which you can find, for example, on page 9, line 19. So for the sake of clarity, in the future the proper and correct translation of what Dr. Simic just said was president of municipal assembly or chairman of municipal assembly, et cetera, but it's not mayor, because that's a completely different term. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please tell me, Dr. Simic, you mentioned the name of the president of the municipal assembly of Bosanski Samac. What was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mato Novic -- Mato Nujic. N-u-i-c [as interpreted]. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that at the time a coalition existed, a multi-party coalition, can you tell us what party did the president of the municipal assembly come from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a coalition. It was more of a partnership that existed between the parties. At the time Mato Nujic, a member of the HDZ, was president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, since the name of Ivo Kobas was mentioned as well with respect to Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it was Ivo Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as I took it, he, without applying appropriate legislative procedure, was removed from office.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, together with his entire cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, instead of those people who then were in the TO staff, who replaced them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The SDA and HDZ put their people into office, into TO staff, and they also appointed head of Territorial Defence staff. And then afterwards, it wasn't the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina any more; it was the Territorial Defence of SDA and HDZ. A member of HDZ was appointed head of -- Chief of Staff, and Alija Fitozovic was appointed his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the time when you completed your military service and when you started working as a physician. When did you start working as a physician in medical centre in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon graduation, in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was your exact title at the medical centre in Samac when you started working?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was head of emergency and general services and ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was director of medical centre in Samac at the time.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mesud Nogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that similar to other institutions the medical centre had multi-ethnic staff, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Nogic, by ethnicity, is what?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what kind of relationship did you have with Dr. Nogic, both professionally and personally?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is Dr. Nogic still employed at the medical centre in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't believe he is any more. However, I think that he still resides in Samac and that he brought his family back to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And until what time did Dr. Nogic remain in the medical centre in Samac as a physician and as an executive? Until what year?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but he remained director of medical centre for quite a while after the war started, until sometime in 1993, I believe. I could be wrong, but I think that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So even during war operations, Dr. Nogic continued working in medical centre in Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was director there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that Samac, just like Bosnia itself, is a multi-ethnic area that nurtured the spirit of ethnic tolerance throughout the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like the entire Yugoslavia did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your youth, while at school, I assume that you had friends among all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was your relationship with your peers from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Very proper, which later led to me choosing a Muslim for a best man at my wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But unfortunately after the break-up of Yugoslavia, I assume that tensions started growing in Samac, just like elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia. Please tell me, when was it that you noticed for the first time that up until then tolerant and proper inter-ethnic and neighbourly relations started deteriorating and changing? What was your personal impression regarding all that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, all of that was initiated in the centres, in large urban centres, Sarajevo, Zagreb, Belgrade perhaps as well, and then it spread to the provinces, elsewhere. With the break-up of Yugoslavia, once the republic started seceding -- and up until then we believed that to be impossible, we believed that it was impossible for somebody to break apart a state that existed for a hundred years, where everybody lived together, went to school together and felt comfortable in. And this led to greater polarisation. And at the time, it was believed that people separated into two groups: Patriots and those who favoured separatism. Patriots wanted to preserve Yugoslavia, and separatists wanted to break it apart. And depending on the method of preserving or breaking apart Yugoslavia, that influenced the events in the field. If the method of break-up was favoured, then that denied the constitution, the system of National Defence, the JNA, and that also basically went against everything that was joint. However, if the system of preserving Yugoslavia was favoured, then people -- then people acted different. There were referendums. There was support expressed to the Yugoslav People's Army and so on. And this spread from the centres to local areas. And in view of the fact that the front was quite near, tensions grew and this in turn led to further polarisation. The war started first in Slovenia, then in Croatia, and then there was a front line some 20 kilometres away in Vukovar. We could hear the combat going on daily. All of this had repercussions in the area of north-western Bosnia. There were refugees streaming in from all ethnic groups. There were soldiers coming to this area. And then the exchanges started between the Yugoslav side and the Croatian side. And all of this frequently went through the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I will interrupt you here and we will come back to that later. You as a young man got involved in politics. You're an educated man, you've read a lot, and so on, so I will put this question to you: You now described patriots to us and those who favoured separatism, and you spoke about one group that wanted their own independent state, and there was another group that wanted to preserve a federal state. And as I said, you read a lot and were involved in politics at the time. Can you tell us whether you can draw any parallels in relation to Northern Ireland in that respect.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There probably are some similarities, however, I'm not an expert and I would not like to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the atmosphere that you described in Samac. I am specifically interested in the following, since you spoke about this in considerable detail: I am now interested in your personal knowledge and your experience about that period in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Samac, that is to say, 1990. As we know, in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina the first multi-party elections were held. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first democratic multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why were these elections different from the previous elections?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because it was the first time that we had political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what was it like before?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Before that, for 50 years we had one party. That is to say, that we did not have a multi-party system. That was the League of Communists, for 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one suggestion: I have a feeling that the interpreters have a problem. Slow -- speak slower, please. I know that you and I speak the same language, but I think that for the same of the transcript it is important for you to speak calmly, slowly, so that the transcript will make sense. You have time. Thank you. So in 1990, if my math doesn't fail me, you were 30 years old. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before 1990, were you engaged in any kind of political work?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you engaged politically in Communist groups, companies, whatever? Please wait for five seconds before you give an answer.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not have any political experience. I was not involved in any kind of political work. However, from 1985 I was a member of the League of Communists, until 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time could a person take up any kind of major position, say, in a company, if he or she was not a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It would be with great difficulty, but there was no absolute rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For example, if there were two doctors applying for the same position -- of course, I don't want to generalise, but, say, on the basis of your own experience -- with the same grades from university university, et cetera, et cetera, one is a member of the Communist Party, the is other one is not. Which one would be admitted?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Advantage would be given to the one who is a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you a believer?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you baptised?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, in 1990 you became a member of a party. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which party is that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you give an approximation in terms of time, not necessarily the accurate date or month but, say, the time of year when you became a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This municipal board of the SDS, was it founded in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Later, yes. But it was established in Gornje Slatina, St. Peter's Day in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Gornje Slatina is near Samac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who was among the founders of the SDS? Just give a few names if you remember.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanko Pivasevic is one of the founders of the Serb Democratic Party. And nowadays he is president in Samac of the municipal board of the SDS. Then there was Stevo Tosic, Marko Tubakovic, et cetera. I was not present. I entered a few months later. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please, I'm just a bit confused by this portion of the evidence. Is the witness saying that this was the founding of the entire party within Bosnia or whether it was a local founding of the party in that area? That might be of some assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Pantelic will -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's not quite clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel will clarify that with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is quite precise explanations in page 16, line 20 and 21. But I would -- I could clarify that. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's clarify this for the Prosecutor and ultimately for the transcript as well. The founding assembly for that municipality was in Gornje Slatina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was the founding assembly of the branch of the Serb Democratic Party for the municipality of Bosanski Samac. It was associated with Jovan Raskovic, because that is the period - this should be known - when there were five democratic parties that were founded. They had different leaderships. And these five Serb Democratic Parties exist until the present day; they were never a single party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned Dr. Jovan Raskovic. Is that the founder of the SDS in Krajina, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the man who created, who invented the Serb Democratic Party. It can be said that he was the first president of the Serb Democratic Party, its founder and ideologue. He established his branches in Krajina, in Bosnia, and in Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. One way or the other, we are talking about a municipal branch, about a municipal board of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which was established in Gornje Slatina in 1990 on St. Peter's Day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We know which date this is, but could you please say which date it is.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I just know it was St. Peter's Day, but I don't know the exact date. It was the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you were not one of the founders of this municipal board?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A few months later you entered the party?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How? Did somebody approach you from this municipal leadership, or was it that you made this decision in some other way? Could you explain your motive. Could you explain to us why you joined the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanko Pivasevic, who was the founder, talked to me - and he is my younger colleague - and the idea was that they needed a man who could win the election and who, together with other parties would create relations of partnerships so that communism could be toppled after 50 years. The first idea, in terms of establishing the Serb Democratic Party and the Croat Democratic Union and the SDA, was to topple communism. Perhaps naively, perhaps not, I accepted to enter the Serb Democratic Party, and they put me at the head of the list for the first elections in the municipality of Samac in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. On that occasion did you acquaint yourself with the programme orientation or, rather, the contents of certain party principles of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, always pause before answering my question. Pause for a few seconds. Because we have to have the question finished. We have to give the interpreters the opportunity to interpret that so that the Trial Chamber can hear this and the Prosecution. And it is only then that you should answer. Please. I know that you have greatly been looking forward to this moment so that you can give your views in respect of all of this after one year of trial, but as you have heard, the Trial Chamber has been very fair and you will have enough time to present everything. So please. I'm asking you the following now: In which way and how did you acquaint yourself with the programme orientation of the SDS in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The programme orientation was brought to me -- no, it wasn't the programme orientation that was brought to me. It was the programme of the SDS that was brought to me. And it was published in all newspapers as, all newspapers that were published then. And there was also a separate bulletin in Bosnia-Herzegovina that published the programmes of all the parties that participated in these first elections. The programme of the Serb Democratic Party was, as the name itself says, was democracy; the preservation of Yugoslavia; the preservation of the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the preservation of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia; respect for the Yugoslav People's Army as the only legitimate and legal force; respect for laws and the constitution of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina; private ownership, because until then private ownership was very scant, barely existent -- private ownership over means of production, until then, that was not the case there was barely any; and denationalisation. That means returning property to their former owners. All the property that was taken away from them when the League of Communists came to head the country in 1945. At that time factories, land, houses, other facilities were nationalised and everything that constituted private property. There was a nationalisation that was carried out, and we advocated denationalisation, that is to say, the return of such property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: And -- and anti-communism was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So as a young man and as a professional, you found yourself in all of this, in this programme?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you headed the election list for the municipal assembly of Bosanski Samac in 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From a few testimonies, we've already heard quite a few details and we've also looked at Official Gazettes. We're not going to go into all of those details now. But tell me briefly - if you remember, of course - what was the outcome of these multi-party elections at local level in Bosanski Samac in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The national parties won a convincing victory. The list of the Serb Democratic Party won almost 98 per cent of the vote, of the Serb vote, that is. The Croat Democratic Union, the HDZ, won a convincing victory among the Croatian population, while the SDA in Samac had a very poor result because the Muslims in Samac primarily voted for the reformed Communist, the SDP, and also for the reformists. So the SDA in Samac did not fair well at all at these first multi-party elections. They won only two seats in the municipal assembly, in the municipal parliament; they did very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and what was the situation at republican level, for the republican parliament? What was the outcome there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Approximately that's the way it was in almost all municipalities. So in the republican parliament, the majority of seats was won precisely by the national parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ. Very few seats were won by the reformed Communists, by the reformists, by the Liberals, et cetera, the SPO, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is this party the SPO?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That is the Serbian Renewal Movement. It was the second or third largest party, headed by Vuk Draskovic, and he managed to win one seat in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina during these first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. One way or the other, at municipal level after these elections, how were the municipal authorities established and among which parties?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Everything that happened at municipal level was reflected from Sarajevo; that was a reflection from what was going on in Sarajevo. So the leaderships of the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS agreed to have relations of partnership, not coalition but relations of partnership for a division of power, which then was supposed to constitute the first non-Communist government after 50 years. Agreement was to share power among the three national parties according to the criteria that they established, and then it depended on the number of seats won in each municipality by one party or the other or the third national party. But one of the principles was that if one party would get the post of the president of the municipal assembly, then the other party would get the office of prime minister of that government, head of the municipal government. And that is how these posts were rotated. So when this agreement was reached, then the municipal parliament was constituted and then there would be a secret ballot on the basis of the rules of procedure of the municipal assembly of Bosanski Samac. And at the proposal of the commission for proposals, namely, the proposals of the national parties, because the national parties established their clubs of MPs in the Municipal Assemblies. In the republican parliament, there was the Club of Deputies of members of parliament as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did I understand you well when you said that this principle of rotation of posts in this partnership -- was the power basically divided according to a certain principle?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to a principle established among the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this principle of key or of quotas was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina anyway, precisely because there are three constituent peoples there in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The concept of key was introduced by the League of Communists, and based on that principle, in Bosnia-Herzegovina all offices were shared between the members of these three peoples. So in one term, president of municipality would be a Serb; in the next term, he would be a Croat; and in the third term, he would be a Muslim; and then we would come back to the beginning of this rotation, so that interests of all three peoples would be satisfied at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, please, after the 1990 elections at the local level, who started inter-party negotiations concerning the organisation of government? Maybe you've already mentioned, but let us say again. These three parties, the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA, did they have certain instructions coming from the republican level as to how the government should be set up?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Those were not really instructions, directions; they were more in the nature of recommendations as to how should the power be shared. And it was addressed to all three parties at the municipal level, and we upheld this recommendation in Bosanski Samac municipality. The clubs of MPs decided about the division of power among themselves. We had a vote and agreed that the president of municipalities should be a member of HDZ, Mato Nujic; vice-president on a voluntary basis of municipal assembly was me; president of the executive council, which means head of the executive government at the municipal level, was Mirko Jovanovic, who described himself as a member of the SDS. However, I never saw his membership booklet, nor did I ask to see it. And his vice-president came from the SDA, and his name was Izet Izetbegovic. And then within the executive branch, the Secretary for Construction came from the HDZ; the Secretary for People's Affairs was a candidate proposed by the SDS, Milos Bogdanovic, who was not a member of the SDS; and then the Secretary of Internal Revenue was Mirko Lukic, who was again nominated by the SDS, although he was not a member of that party, and so on and so on. One of the posts that had to be agreed between the parties was also the Chief of Staff of Territorial Defence, and that post was awarded to the SDS, because in the past that post was held by a Croat, Ivo Dragicevic. And we didn't ask that he be replaced. We supported his appointment as commander of the Territorial Defence in 1990, and he had our support all the way until the beginning of the war. I haven't finished yet. And as regards the chief of police in Bosanski Samac, that office was awarded to HDZ -- or rather, they appointed Ivo Dragicevic head of police. He was a Croat. And Ivo Kobas was commander of the TO staff. So I made a mistake. I got them confused. And I would like to set this clear now. Ivo Dragicevic, although he was a member of the HDZ had the support of the SDS; however, before the war broke out, he was forcibly removed from office and that office was taken over by Dragan Lukac forcibly, who became chief of police then, who testified in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. These are all political issues, but they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, you used the word "forcibly" in terms of the removal of the one person, Mr. Dragicevic, and then you used the word "forcibly" again in terms of the office being taken over by Mr. Dragan Lukac. Could you just explain very briefly what you mean by "forcibly" in those two circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards every executive post within the municipality, head of police was a political appointee who had professionals working under him. So he was a political appointee and then professionals performed various duties. And parties wanted Ivo Dragicevic to take that office, and without party's approval no executive can be removed from office. Sometime around 12th of April, and perhaps even earlier, the leadership of SDA and SDS [as interpreted] coalition started persecuting Ivo Dragicevic and appointed Dragan Lukac to the office without consent of the third party. And at that time that represented forcible takeover of the police station, because Dragan Lukac did not have a consent from the Serbian side to take that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's just make a correction and to remind you. Were you, in fact, referring to Vinko Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Vinko Dragicevic. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. In order to set the transcript clear, let's put it this way: Mr. Vinko Dragicevic, a Croat by ethnicity, was head of municipal SUP, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivo Kobas, a Croat by ethnicity, was commander of TO staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's just clarification for the transcript so that we have proper names and titles here. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, perhaps to assist Mr. Pantelic, I wonder if he could look at line 17 from page 25. Did the witness mean to say that around the 12th of April, the leadership of the SDA and SDS started persecuting Ivo Dragicevic and appointed Dragan Lukac to the office?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend, although in politics everything is possible, you know, so that this combination too. But I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, there's an error in the transcript, so let's clarify that as well. You spoke about the time period around the 12th of April, prior to the breakout of hostilities in Samac. Which two parties basically in an illegal way, in contrary to the municipal statute, put Dragan Lukac into the office?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was the coalition of the SDA and HDZ. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. So there were certain principles that were set out. The SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA had a sort of a local agreement regarding the distribution of posts. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this inter-party agreement, was it basically founded on a consensus?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In reality, does that mean that when one party has a candidate for a post in the municipal administration and a third party is against that nominee, that that person cannot be appointed? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in April of 1992 there were at least two examples where that inter-party agreement was violated at a municipal level in Bosanski Samac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you held the post of vice-president of municipal assembly as a volunteer. Please tell me, what was the scope of your responsibilities, and what did you do as vice-president of the municipal assembly in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did this on a voluntary basis, meaning that I did not have an office in the municipal assembly building, since in 1991 I worked in Doboj, which is 70 kilometres from Samac, I was attending a residency training there. And in 1992 I worked in Tuzla, which is some 100 kilometres away. Due to my professional responsibilities, I seldom found time to come to the municipal assembly and acquaint myself with what was going on there regularly. However, there was no need for that at all because I had no duties other than being an assemblyman in the assembly because representatives of Serb people were in various committees and secretariats, and they were able to duly represent their electorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the member of the municipal board of SDS in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1990 it was Stevo Tosic and Dr. Stanko Pivasevic; both of them held that post. And in 1991, I was elected to that post, namely, president of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the exact date, just what season it was. Summer? Fall?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it was fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While performing your volunteer duties as vice-president of the municipal assembly, did you as an executive of the municipal assembly have any perks? Did you have a limousine, a bodyguard, a driver? Did you have any particular privileges that went with that office?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, there were no benefits or privileges attached to that office. I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So basically you continued doing what you used to do before. You continued living like you lived before, except that you, due to your political activities, also were appointed to that post as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please briefly explain to us this: After the municipal assembly was established in 1990 between the three parties - HDZ, SDA, and SDS - an agreement was reached between them and then sessions of the municipal assembly were held. Can you tell us something about those sessions. Who prepared the agenda? Who prepared material that was to be analysed at a session and so on? Can you please describe what a typical session looked like. How was everything prepared for it? Can you just give us an idea as to how that looked at a municipal level.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: President of the assembly would convene a session and send out agenda and material for that session. The work of the assembly was regulated by the statute of the municipal assembly, and the municipal assembly at the time and later on as well had very few authorities, mostly those that had to do with infrastructure, utilities, and so on. Whereas, everything else boiled down to just formal reports, and I will explain what I mean by this. The municipal assembly was not allowed to interfere into affairs of the Ministry of the Interior because there was a government at republican level and there was a Minister of Defence at that level, which regulated these affairs. The municipal assembly was not allowed to interfere in financial matters and revenue administration because at the republican level there was a Minister of Finance, who through municipal offices and financial police regulated all of these matters. So the entire financial sector was the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. Healthcare was regulated by the Minister for Health. Primary and secondary health services were organised by him as well; meaning that he organised medical centres, hospital, the healthcare network as well. The financing for the healthcare services was performed at the republican level. Education was organised and controlled by the Minister of Education. He appointed principals in schools. He paid out salaries for staff. He organised schools, faculties, kindergartens, and so on, so this area was organised by the ministry at the republican level as well. Agriculture, which is one of the most important spheres in Posavina was regulated by the Minister of Agriculture. Waterworks -- there are two rivers in our area -- were regulated by the Minister for Waterworks. Forestry, once again, was regulated by the Minister for Forestry. The economy was regulated by the Minister for Economy. So there was basically not a single sphere that wasn't covered by government at the republican level, and therefore the scope of responsibilities of municipal assembly was very narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, I'm interested in what a session of the municipal assembly looked like. First of all, tell me what -- you say that the president of the municipal assembly sends the agenda, et cetera, et cetera. Now I'm asking you who in the municipal assembly prepares materials, drafts decisions, various documents, et cetera. Tell us about the staff of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These are the organs within which is the secretariat, and it takes care of all the operative work. There is always a secretary employed there who is a lawyer, and he always bears in mind the fact that these decisions have to be in accordance with the law. It is almost always the municipal government, the members of the municipal government, that propose these bills and these documents to the assembly because the assembly is the legislative branch of government and it needs to -- and the executive needs to coordinate with the legislation so that it can carry out its functions. Individual assemblymen can also propose the agenda. The agenda is first adopted by the municipal parliament. And if it obtains a democratic majority, that is to say, 51 per cent, then that particular agenda is adopted. Then there is a discussion, there are answers, there are conclusions, and then the president of the municipal assembly asks for a vote to be taken. The assemblymen say whether they want to vote in public, that is to say, by raising their hands, or if they want to have a secret ballot, and then voting is organised. If a democratic majority is obtained, 51 per cent, then such a decision is considered adopted. It is the organs - that is to say secretariats - that write this out. Lawyers are there on the staff, and it is their duty to have everything kept in accordance with the law. Then they bring it to the president of the municipal assembly for his signature. Then this decision is further channelled to the executive authorities. In the executive authorities, there are professionals. In every secretariat there had to be highly educated professionals who were in charge of bearing in mind in accordance with the law on the administration whether every decision is lawful or not. If a decision is not lawful, then it was returned to parliamentary procedure again, or they asked for an opinion from the competent legal services. Legal people know this better than I do, in which way this is done. And they were quite literally in charge of having every decision of the municipal assembly sufficiently lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us show this by way of an example. A certain municipal tax is introduced. Now, in the municipal government, in the municipal executive committee, which service, which staff, is in charge of drafting a proposal on municipal tax?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In the situation of Samac - because this is a small municipality and the administration was always kept at the lowest level possible - this was done by the Secretary of the Economy. The proposal for this kind of tax -- for example, companies were taxed. Then also outdoor cafes were taxed. Then also the number of chairs in various cafes and restaurants was taxed, and so on and so forth. This proposal of the Secretariat for Economic Activities is put forth to the administration organs, and then administration organs make a proposal to the assembly. If the assemblymen agree that this decision can be passed, it is then returned to the executive once again. They look at how lawful it is, and then the decision is implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the president of the municipal assembly is an office that is not directly related to the preparation, analysis, and the adoption procedure for certain documents from the domain of the activity of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How often after 1990 in this multi-party parliament of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac did you have sessions of the municipal assembly, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Approximately once every two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during that same period of time, how often were sessions of the executive council held?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Far more often. I think every seven days. Sometimes even more often; sometimes even every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the executive council have certain powers by way of adopting certain decisions or regulations from its own provenance of work?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything that is regulated by statute and law. However, the municipal executive council was responsible to the parliament, but according to certain enactments it also had its responsibilities towards the republican government and the ministries. So there is this line within the executive branch of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The decisions of the executive council, were they also binding for the population, or rather, various sectors of the society and economy?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this is a kind of, conditionally speaking, in order to give an illustration -- that this would perhaps be a kind of by-law in the sense of a decree, decision, or conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At the municipal level these are already legal matters, and I cannot say much about that. This is the municipal government, the municipal authority. Everything is regulated by laws and decrees, and they indeed have a broad scope for action within the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me - we have a minute until the break - tell me, the way in which the vote takes place in the municipal assembly, tell me, after how many members of parliament were there in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think about 40 assemblymen, but I'm not absolutely certain. Not approximately, it was 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A decision required a majority?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you, the SDS, not immediately make a coalition with the Serb parties?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I wanted to correct myself first. At that time the municipal parliament had 50 members, 50 assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I asked you why you did not form a coalition with Serb parties immediately. The SDS, why didn't it do that, the SDS and other parties?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Parties cannot be divided into Serb parties and other parties. I could only divide them into patriotic parties and some other parties. However, relations of partnership between the national parties were primarily based on anti-communism and agreement was reached between these -- among these three parties to establish the first government after 50 years between and among the three parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take our break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just last question before the break. If you have another question, maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's already 11.01. Think of the interpreters, please. They need their break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break and return at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Examination-in-chief continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before the break we were talking about the principles of work of the municipal assembly and how preparations are carried out. We also discussed some aspects of political partnership among the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS at local level. From the multi-party elections in 1990 onwards in the municipality of Bosanski Samac until the autumn of 1991, how would you describe your inter-party relations and the atmosphere in carrying out your political duties, that is to say, among these three political parties, what is your view regarding this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I would like to explain what the real situation was in the municipal parliament in 1990. That is to say, the municipal parliament had 50 assemblymen; the HDZ had 21 MPs; the Serb Democratic Party 17; the SDA [Realtime transcript read in error"17"] had 2; the Liberals had 1; the Reformists had 4; and the Reform Communists had 5. I am mentioning all of this so that I could show that the patriotic bloc, that is to say the bloc that advocated Yugoslavia could have formed a government on its own, without the HDZ and the SDA, because we had almost 30 assemblymen. So we could vote in favour of any decision basically and we could appoint officials from the SDS, the Liberal Party, the Reformist party, and the Reform Communist Party only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Intervention. It's on page 35, line 15. It has the 17 had 2. It has no meaning, so I believe it was the SDA, but maybe it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said that the SDA had two members of parliament in the municipal assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please proceed, Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: So we could have formed a government on our own, and the HDZ and the SDA would not have had a single official in the municipality of Samac. However, respecting our relations of partnership at republic level, we made it possible for them to share power on a footing of equality with the Serb Democratic Party, expecting this anti-Communist bloc to achieve some results and that we would not destroy what was most important to us, and that was the state. However, the situation started changing as time went by. Some witnesses spoke about this here as well. However, polarisation in the municipal parliament between the HDZ and the SDA, as opposed to the patriotic bloc, became ever-more pronounced. And when they could not carry through decisions at the level of the municipal parliament, they did not even convene any sessions, because it is the president of the assembly that convenes the municipal parliament sessions. They made decisions on their own. So inter alia, they themselves reached a decision on changing the head of the staff of the Territorial Defence. On their own, they passed a decision on changing the head of the Public Security Station and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1991 the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina became highly tense. The war in Croatia started. And bearing in mind the fact that Bosanski Samac is on the banks of the Sava River, only about 50 metres away from Croatian territory, what did you personally notice during the year of 1991 as regards transportation and also certain incidents in Bosanski Samac? What were your personal observations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that the co-accused will speak to a greater extent about this, but I can say that already in 1991 Serbs no longer crossed the bridge in Samac and none of the Serbs went to Croatia any longer. From Croatia though, every day Serb refugees were coming in en masse from all parts of the Republic of Croatia, notably from the zone of war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, there was traffic primarily between Croats and Croats, and Muslims on the one hand and Croats on the other hand, or Muslims and Croats together, but the Serbs could not use that bridge or road in Croatia, not even for their private companies or did they dare go on behalf of socially-owned companies. Soldiers of the ZNG already started coming across; that's what the Croatian army was called at the time. They were crossing in uniform and with weapons. They appeared in the town of Samac. All of this gave rise to tensions, major tensions among all three ethnic groups; among the Serb people for the most part. Then information was coming in that Croat volunteers were going to the front line in Croatia en masse, that they were being trained there to participate in the war, that they were obtaining uniforms and weapons, that they were training officers, and that all of this is then returned to the area of Posavina. Then information came in to the effect that all Croat villages already have established units, their own units armed, linked up with officers of their own, and then also people were talking in town about this and then checkpoints were set up in Croat villages in the territory of the municipality of Samac and throughout Posavina. So Serbs could not longer go to Croat territory or could they cross through Croat villages, absolutely not at nighttime. Then also bunkers were cropping up like mushrooms at the boundaries of all Croat villages. I saw this with my very own eyes. This was particularly pronounced between Hasici and Kruskovo Polje. When the inhabitants of Kruskovo Polje asked the inhabitants of Hasici: "Why are you building bunkers that are so obvious, that are so striking" --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have the Exhibit P9. This is a map of Samac and surrounding villages, so that maybe Dr. Simic can show us the exact positions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, which particular map would you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think A. A will be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please take the pointer. Not the felt pen but the metal pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The pointer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You don't have to mark this, but when you are telling us what you saw, please just point to it with a pencil.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the area of Hasici, and it is around this village in the direction of the Serbian villages that quite large bunkers were erected, and these were visible from the road. Towards the end of 1991, information arrived to the effect that the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina had been established. It covered the territory of eight Bosnian municipalities, and I cannot indicate this territory on this map. These were Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Odzak, Modrica, Samac, Orasje, and Gradacac. After this, tensions mounted even more because this resembled a sort of state that wanted to annex itself to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Take P9A and we could have Exhibit P12, which depicts the area of Posavina, so that we could better follow the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. You were talking about the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina. Could you please show us what municipalities made up this community.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Modrica, Odzak, Samac, Orasje, and Gradacac. This is the area that the Croats in Bosanska Posavina considered to be theirs and which they wanted to annex to the Republic of Croatia. In several conversations I had Mato Nujic told me this. He was the president of the municipal assembly. And Filipovic, who was the president of the Croatian Democratic Union -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- just gone some way to answering the query that I'm about the raise. But I wonder if Mr. Pantelic could clarify whether the position -- when the witness says "Croats in Bosanska Posavina considered this area to be theirs," this Croatian municipality or whatever, is the witness referring to a political programme on the part of the HDZ? Is it his assessment of the general consensus amongst the Croat population? Is it a certain group of Croats? Does he know specifically when he says "Croats" who he's talking about in particular? That might be of interest to the Chamber and certainly of interest to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly my assumption is that Dr. Simic will explain that, because he mentioned the president of HDZ, Croatian party, in Samac as well as the president of municipal assembly, also Croat. And probably during this conversation we shall hear more about that. But I will direct the -- Dr. Simic towards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Dr. Simic, as regards these meetings and what my learned friend has just asked.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These were conversations held in the office of the president of the municipal assembly. He used to work in the health centre with me. He was employed as a lawyer there, and he worked with my father as well, so he had a paternal attitude toward me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mato Nujic. He treated me like a son. He was a lawyer and I was a doctor, so I don't know enough about law, but he advised me or else he tried to justify his actions. He told me that this was Croatian territory and that they had established the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina. He also said that at the head of this community was Iko Stanic, that its seat was in Derventa, that they had established their own army which they then called the Croatian Defence Council, and that they considered this to be sovereign territory of the Republic of Croatia. I thought that this was an overambitious line of thinking of an overambitious local politician and that something like this was impossible. I thought it was impossible for Yugoslavia to break up. I thought it was impossible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to break up, and I thought it was especially impossible for a territory to be broken up into such small local areas. However, in early 1992 everyday events showed that their intentions were serious. Relatively soon in early 1992, the Serb population were dismissed from their jobs in all these municipalities and little by little they moved out. They moved to areas which they believed to be safer, and many of them moved in the direction of the Samac municipality. In early 1992 the Serbian population of Orasje, Brod, Derventa, and especially Odzak, where they were grouped in Serb local communes, many of them no longer went to work. Then road blocks were set up, skirmishes broke out. There were conflicts, and there was forcible takeover of towns. Bosanski Brod was taken over, and the Serbs were expelled and made to go to the Serbian part of the territory of Bosanski Brod. After this part of the Croatian army crossed the River Sava and perpetrated the massacre in Sijekovac, and this was on the territory of Bosanski Brod, very close to Samac as the close flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll come to this, doctor, but could you please indicate on the map which is on the ELMO where Bosanski Brod is.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Here is Sijekovac and here is Samac. The town of Bosanski Brod was taken over by the Muslim Croat forces and the Serbian population was expelled from that area or else they were imprisoned. After that the town of Derventa was taken over and there were clashes there. In Odzak there was a large percentage of Croats, so that there were no conflicts in the town. The Serbs simply didn't enter the town any more. And as for the villages, in Orasje there was a large percentage of Croats, so that the Serbs moved out of that town and crossed over to the territory of the municipality of Samac, to Batkusa and Obudovac. In Gradacac the Serbs also moved out and the town was taken over by Croatian and Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, I have to interrupt you. This was in the spring of 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to an earlier period of time chronologically, and then we shall come back to this later, simply for the sake of a logical narrative and in order to present the facts. I wish to ask you specifically what your opinion was about the atmosphere in Bosanski Samac itself. I'm speaking of late 1991 and early 1992. What was the relation between neighbours and friends? What were their relations? Were there any ethnic divisions that were noticeable?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, tensions mounted daily. There was ethnic division, and people were concentrated in Croatian or Serbian municipalities. From day to day there was less and less confidence because some thought that Yugoslavia should collapse, that there should no longer be a JNA, while the patriotic side believed that Yugoslavia should survive, that a political solution should be found, and that the JNA should be the only army securing peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking of this, please tell us in late 1991 and early 1992, were you called for military exercises as a JNA reservist?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. I was in the medical corps, and I was called for exercises on a regular basis ever since I completed my army service. I received call-up notes, and I responded every time there was an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In relation to the previous period, did you notice any changes in the ethnic make-up of the reservists who responded to these calls for exercises?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were far fewer Croats now, and this was very noticeable. The Muslims responded as they had before. One couldn't say that there were no Muslims in the JNA and that they did not perform all the tasks assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, were you called up to the 4th JNA Detachment?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to October 1991, when in the middle of that month there were certain tensions and a serious split in the republican parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I would like to know now is what you know about this personally, and later on I will put a few more questions in connection with the impact of this event on political developments and political relations on the local level in Bosanski Samac. So in brief, what do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that a great deal of us followed this on television. This was a very difficult situation in which two people were -- two peoples were outvoting the third nation. They were denying something that existed for almost 100 years, and that was the state of Yugoslavia, and at the same time trying to create something that never existed before, because Bosnia and Herzegovina never existed as a state before, especially not within those borders. At the same time, they completely ignored the fact that there was another nation living there from ancient times, perhaps a nation older than any other nation with that status nowadays. So it was a very difficult situation which led to a great many divisions on the ground and provoked dissatisfaction among the population and at the same time led to polarisation between patriots and separatists. I am using the term "patriots" because it wasn't only the Serbs that wanted Yugoslavia to remain intact, but there were also those from the category of Yugoslavs. Then there were Jews, Romas, and a great deal of Muslims in Bosanski Samac, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a portion of Croats who supported Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At a local level in inter-party contacts in October and November of 1991, what were you able to observe? Was your cooperation regarding assembly affairs the same, or were there any changes there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. The atmosphere wasn't the same as before. People started rooting for their causes. They commented on the issue of whether Yugoslavia would continue to exist or not, on who would win in Croatia, whether this army or that army would win in Vukovar, who had greater casualties on a daily basis, was it this army or that army, and so on people started splitting into two blocs and it was evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, were you able to notice any changes in surrounding villages on the roads and so on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
