utterances.text: Barricades, or rather, checkpoints were set up on the roads in all Croat villages. Some unknown soldiers manned those checkpoints, wearing insignia that wasn't familiar, and they also had a particular type of conduct that wasn't known until then. Residents avoided those villages and those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to go into historical topics, but do you have any information and could you tell the Trial Chamber who held the power in 1941 in the territory of Bosanska Posavina, as well as during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: During the Second World War, this was -- this area was ruled by Independent State of Croatia, NDH, Independent State of Croatia. It is a well-known fact that during World War II they sided with Hitler and that their units were called Ustasha units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Based on your daily contacts with people, could you tell us what was their impression regarding the emergence of uniformed individuals, barricades, checkpoints, and so on.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This reminded them of the Second World War, when Ustashas tried to destroy the population en masse, and this took place some 70 -- or rather, 70 to 80 kilometres as the crow flies from Samac was a site where some 700.000 Serbs, Jews, and Romas were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, the sufficient time does not include history, which is not relevant to the issues in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, it's to be cut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, Dr. Simic, I asked you a specific question: In 1991 can you please describe to us what was the predominant feeling among the Serb residents. How did they feel about this increasing arming of the other nations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. On the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, as far as we know, a plebiscite of Serb people was held. Can you tell us what was the purpose of this plebiscite and what was decided then.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The plebiscite of Serb people was held. Other nations also could have participated. And the question that was to be decided was whether they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia or not. I have to say that in that area in Serb local communes, Serbs in -- almost -- Serbs almost fully voted in favour for remaining in Yugoslavia, whereas in the territory of Bosanski Samac itself, the town, 75 to 80 per cent of all citizens who voted, voted in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, in the beginning of January was there something created in the Serb community in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Serb assembly in Bosanski Samac was created at that time, and then later on the Serb republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you just bear with me for a second. I have some notes from my colleague regarding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is an error in the transcript, page 47, line 9. It was not Serb assembly in Bosanski Samac that was created at that time. It was the Serb assembly on a level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I will clarify that for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, let's clarify this. After the plebiscite in the beginning of January, you said that something was created. Can you tell us again what.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of January, 1992 the Serbian republic was created and proclaimed, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact. And later on it was named Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And prior to that, what was established?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The people's assembly of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, how was the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac in Peligecevo established at the end of February 1992? How did that come about? And specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before that answer, if you look at the transcript, page 48, line 3, at 4 we haven't got the answer interpreted. Maybe he wasn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm grateful for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question. So at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the People's Assembly of the Serb people was created. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. We are now focussing on the end of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: What is meant by the expression "at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina"? What ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have to clarify the English expression, which doesn't seem to be quite precise. Let me ask you this way: Was the People's Assembly of the Serb people created for the territory of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was created for the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in that decision on creating the People's Assembly of the Serb nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was defined that that organ was associated with a certain territory.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was defined in that way; however, this is a legal issue, and I cannot go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a certain recommendation of the People's Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina on creating Serb municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now we are dealing with the end of February 1992. And can you tell us, please, how was the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac in Peligicevo created?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: So first there was a plebiscite of Serb people held and the Serb population voted in large numbers in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia. After that a recommendation was adopted by the People's Assembly of Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish Serb municipalities on the basis of the right to self-determination and secession. Following that, in all Serb local communes in that area town meetings were held, as they were called in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. I'm not sure that that can be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All right. That means then residents of every local commune or village would be called to gather, usually in culture halls, and a proposal was presented to them and they were asked to vote on it. Residents voted by raising their hands. The question they were asked was whether you are in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia, and they would vote in favour or against it. And then the second question put to them was whether the citizens were in favour of creating Serb municipalities in Serb areas, and they would have, again, to vote in favour or against it. Based on their votes, in the territory of Posavina, representatives of Serb local communes gathered and created Serb municipality Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo in formation. They created municipal assembly, elected executive council, appointed assemblymen who participated in elections, and that parliament has existed since then and exists even today with a certain change in territory, because later on Pelagicevo was proclaimed a municipality, as was Srpsko Orasje, whereas Odzak remained a different municipality, as did Vukosavlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was the founding session held of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo and where.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was held at the memorial centre in Bosanski Samac at the end of February 1992. The exact date can be seen in the decision that was adopted then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who attended this founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was attended by Serb assemblymen who were elected at the first parliamentary elections in 1990 from the municipalities of Bosanski Samac, Odzak, Orasje, and Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And these Serb assemblymen, from which political parties did they come from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They came from the Serb Democratic Party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, the SDP, the Liberals, the Party of the Reform Forces, and I think that there were representatives of citizens who were not in any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that occasion were rules of procedure for the work of this assembly adopted?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that occasion was the president of the municipal assembly elected?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was elected president?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: As president of the first assembly, it was Ilija Ristic - Dr. Ilija Ristic who was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at this Official Gazette. You have these decisions here, so we can deal with these questions more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam Usher, Exhibit P124 and ter. This is the Official Gazette of the Municipality of Samac, where a certain number of decisions were published, including the general decision of the foundation, establishment, of Serbian municipalities. So we can go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that Official Gazette number 1, Dr. Simic? Do you have number 1 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at page 4 of the B/C/S version. Please take a look at the upper right-hand corner, number 4. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's ERN number 00479560.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So tell me, Dr. Simic, who was then elected vice-president of the assembly of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Dusan Tanasic was elected. Dusan Tanasic, T-a-n-a-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at Article 8 of this decision on the establishment of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what would you have to say by way of comment with regard to Article 8? Do you remember whether this was discussed and what the objective was of adopting this kind of formulation? What did this pertain to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This pertained to the following: Everything that was being established by the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina can be withdrawn if the decision on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina is withdrawn. If, on the other hand, there is no such decision, then the Serb people ask that there is separation by peaceful means between the Serb territory and other territories. Until such a moment when there would be this separation, all officials in joint assemblies would remain at their posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you be able to comment upon Article 9, in terms of the technical aspect, as to how it was envisaged. For certain separations to take place in a material, legal, and property sense.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This Article 9 is self-explanatory. It was envisaged that mixed commissions be established, that there should be peaceful agreement, and that these mixed commissions should do whatever was supposed to be done by way of documents and everything else that both sides were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At this gathering, was there any mention of a forcible takeover of power, any armed actions, or revenge against members of other ethnic groups in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. That was never discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was the basic point of these mixed commissions an attempt by the Serb and Muslim and Croat sides to divide by peaceful means the funds and the material assets in this specific municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the principle governing these mixed commissions. Who was supposed to be a member of these mixed commissions, those mentioned in Article 9?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I am being asked to comment on Article 9. I'm not a lawyer, and I did not write these decisions of the mixed commission. I assume that it is the representatives of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Article 6, can you comment on the objective of the adoption of this Article 6 within this decision. If you recall, of course.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I would like legal people to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on page 7 of that Official Gazette, you see the decision on the election of members of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The English version should be -- yes, ERN number 00479568.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This decision, as its title says, refers to the election of members of the executive council. Tell me, since it was adopted at the second session on the 28th of March, 1992 -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At this first founding meeting at the memorial centre towards the end of February, do you remember was there any reference to the establishment of an executive council, or was this just the founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: What is most important and what happens at an assembly is written down as conclusions and published in the Official Gazette. So now I can only comment upon what is written in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, towards the end of February 1992, was any reference made to annexation to some Serb autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you elected vice-president of the Serb autonomous area of Northern Bosnia towards the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I attended that meeting; however, I must say that this SAO district, as far as I know, was not constituted at all, nor did it ever function, nor did it ever pass any decisions. Nobody ever handed me a decision stating that I was its vice-president. The municipality of Samac did not adopt any decision either to the effect that it would belong to any one of the SAO areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As you say, this SAO Northern Bosnia practically never functioned.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the activity of the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac in Pelagicevo after the founding assembly? Were there any sessions? Were there any meetings? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the next session after February was held in March, and then the one after that was held in March 1992, and the one after that was held in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So practically from February --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: February, from the end of February, when the founding assembly was held, until March 1992, there were no assembly activities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So more or less this was a mere declaration, rather than an effected decision?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have a problem with translation that you see?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. My answer had not been typed in yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what was the reaction of the other two constituent peoples in Samac? I mean, on the basis of some of the personal contacts you had, in respect of the establishment of the Serb municipality.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that the policy was unchanged. Regardless of the consequences, the policy at local level of the HDZ and the SDA worked in the direction of creating an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say, regardless of what the Serb people did and the extent to which they protested and complained, they never deviated from the establishment of an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your personal knowledge regarding the activities of the International Community, precisely at that time, in 1991, in December 1991 and January and February 1992, from the press or from some other contacts? Are you aware of the Lisbon negotiations and a certain agreement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That time, the beginning of 1992 all the way up to the summer of 1992, is a period of time when the Lisbon agreement was being referred to as well as the Cutilheiro plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who did you discuss this with at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, at the outset this was published by all newspapers. It was on TV. It was discussed among people at all levels. And this was a ray of hope that we in Bosnia-Herzegovina would perhaps be smart and that there would not be a war. The European Community worked rather intensively on this plan, on the Lisbon agreement, and at that time it represented a solution for all three peoples. We heard yesterday as well that three years later the Dayton Agreement was signed, which differs very little from the Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, let us focus on your personal knowledge and on testimony concerning the time that we are discussing, so that we would not deviate from the line of testimony. What you referred to are generally known facts, and we're going to leave that for some other occasion. So now I'm asking you once again: Among the parties that constituted the government at local level, the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS, was any reference made to the resolution of certain political tensions, both at political level and beyond?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How often and with who did you communicate for the most part? I assume that you then, as the president of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Physically I was absent, so I took part in these discussions to a lesser extent. But the president of the executive council and other assemblymen of the Serb Democratic Party had the opportunity of conducting such talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where were you when you were physically absent?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was doing my residency in Tuzla at the time, so that means this is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. But to a large extent your co-workers gave you information as to what was going on. You were president of the municipal board of the SDS, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These were unofficial talks at micro level, and basically nothing depended on that because the kind of agreement that is reached at top level is usually transmitted to micro level. There was only one inter-party discussion at an official level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time the president of the executive committee of the Bosanski Samac municipality, which was established after the elections of 1990, was Mirko Jovanovic, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge and did he inform you of how cooperation in his institution, the executive committee, was functioning in those first few months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He informed the entire municipal assembly and all the deputies. There were very few personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he or did others who were active in the municipal organs of this municipality at that time, did they draw your attention to certain issues or problems or to tensions they were faced with in their work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you still need --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. Thank you. Thank you. Sorry, Ms. Usher. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us, did you find out from your colleagues or friends anything about the way in which business was conducted, whether there were any political tensions and what people thought and what your personal observations were?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Individuals meant nothing at the time. Their work was made very difficult, and starting from the 10th of April, they didn't even go to work because they didn't feel safe. The undermining of their work took place at all levels. The decisions they were supposed to be implementing on the territory influenced by the HDZ and the SDA simply could not be implemented. Then they stopped going to those areas at all. I am referring to secretaries, inspectors, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What inspectors?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The inspectors working in the municipalities, inspectors mostly of the Internal Revenue Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume there were no police inspectors employed in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the second session of the Serb municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo, on the 28th of March, 1992, certain members of the executive council were elected. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you nominate Stevan Todorovic as chief of the Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who nominated him, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He was nominated by Lazar Stanisic. But I think he was also supported by Ilija Ristic, the then-president of the municipal assembly. I can say that the Serb Democratic Party opposed Stevan Todorovic being appointed to any post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, on page 58 and where you have an answer, "Individuals meant nothing at the time," what does the -- Dr. Simic mean by "individuals"? It's a very diffused concept. Could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the way this was interpreted into English, when you were asked as to whether your colleagues informed you of their problems at work, you said this did not take place on an individual level but through institutions. Could you explain this to Judge Lindholm. Can you explain how this functioned at the local level in relation to these various secretariats and people's posts and the difficulties they had at work, who they informed of this and how all this functioned while you were the deputy president of the municipal assembly elected at the elections.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The president of the executive council chaired the meetings of the executive council, and this was a body in which information was exchanged among the members. Then the president of the executive council informed the assembly, which numbered 50 assemblymen, and he presented his impressions and suggestions to the assembly. If he wanted to inform the party, he would come to the deputies club, the meeting of the deputies club, when invited by a political party, and this took place in the municipal assembly building. The Serb Democratic Party had 17 assemblymen, and then he would inform them of his impressions, his conclusions, his suggestions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The sense, Your Honour, was of -- of course that's my understanding of the previous answer of Dr. Simic that individuals were not in charge to do anything at the same time when the institutions were there. That means that there were no private lines of professional work, I mean, between one department of the -- one municipal functioner and someone from the authorities of the municipality. It's, rather, a relation between -- ex officio between the functioner in one department and the next level, which is executive board or municipal assembly. That was the sense of his explanation previously, if that satisfied your inquiry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the assembly of the 28th of March, 1992, when you said that the SDS opposed the appointment of Stevan Todorovic as chief of the Public Security Station. I am a little bit confused when you say that. Was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party expelled him after the first parliamentary elections. He was expelled from the party. He was not allowed to participate on the list of candidates. And from that time, the party did not count on him in any way whatsoever. The proposal, or rather, the nominees of the Serb Democratic Party were professionals. Pero Stevic, Milan Stankovic, Petrovic - I've forgotten his first name - men like that, but not Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When the list was drawn up in 1992 for the local elections, was there -- I won't call it a conflict, but were there any tensions between you and Stevan Todorovic? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That was one of my conditions. I said if I was at the head of the list, he could not be in it because I knew him -- I had known him for a certain time as a patient, and I didn't want him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How do you mean as a patient?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: As an alcoholic, a drug addict, someone addicted to pills.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. At this session of the 28th of March, what group nominated him? Was this a fraction among the Serb deputies or assemblymen? Were you outvoted? Did you remain in the minority? Can you explain this process. How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At the Serbian assembly there were 50 assemblymen from different parties, and within the Serbian Democratic Party there were also various groups. Whether interest groups or other factions, it was impossible to have a unanimous opinion, so that some people insisted that it should be him. And during the secret ballot, he was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the period during the first few months of 1992, did you continue to be the deputy president of the Bosanski Samac Municipal Assembly elected in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any sessions of this assembly in that composition?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, unless I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And why not? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because the HDZ and the SDA did not have a parliamentary majority, and they could not push through the decisions that suited them. That's why the president never convened the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How, then, did the executive council of that municipality elected in 1992, where the vice-president was Izet Izetbegovic and where others were in the municipal secretariats, how did it function? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it functioned with ever-greater difficulties throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this period, as the president of the SDS municipal committee or board, did you together with the other Serb assemblymen or other circles of people of Serb ethnicity draw up any plans about takeover of power in Bosanski Samac? You personally, I mean.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any of your close associates from the SDS or from the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac drawing up plans which would include a takeover of power by forcible means in the Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have any secret talks or relations with the JNA units that were stationed in the territory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts or any plans with the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In those first few months of 1992, did you recruit your acquaintances or certain young people as members of commando units?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you, together with Stevan Todorovic in these first few months of 1992, have any meetings or talks about establishing a Serbian police in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you put forward any initiatives in connection with the establishment of a Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly what your role was. First, explain to us what the Crisis Staff was, in fact, on the basis of what you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is actually the municipal assembly under conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the previous period, during the former Yugoslavia, would there have been a Crisis Staff at the local level and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was always established in times of crisis, when there was an earthquake, a flood, a big fire, whenever there was any sort of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what in essence was the purpose of that body?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: To get through the period until conditions were created for the convening of the entire assembly. All decisions would then have to be tabled before the entire assembly and re-adopted by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's time for a break. And then in the afternoon we shall start with another part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall have our lunch break and continue our proceedings at 14.30 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief is continuing with Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, before the break we touched upon the Crisis Staff. Now, please tell me, based on your information, how was the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac established?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: After the founding -- after one of the sessions in March, it was decided that should it be needed, a Crisis Staff should be established if the war breaks out in the territory of Bosanska Posavina. President and vice-president of municipality and the chairman of the municipal board of SDS were tasked with implementing this. However, we believed that there wouldn't be a war, and therefore we didn't do much in terms of making consultations with respect to the Crisis Staff. Then there was a meeting of the executive council of the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac in Pelagicevo under formation was held, and the situation was described as dramatic there. And based on that information on the 14th and 15th of April, I believe, it was insisted that a Crisis Staff should be established if there are any war operations in the area. Possible appointees to the Crisis Staff were discussed, and its general structure, however, the Crisis Staff itself was not established. The war broke out on the 16th and 17th of April. We did not have a Crisis Staff, nor did we have a stamp of the Crisis Staff. And somewhere between the 17th and 19th of April, we had consultations with assemblymen of the municipal assembly and -- with participation of the people from the Ministry of Defence, because people had been mobilised and they were sent to the front line, which was some 70 kilometres long. And with consent of patriotic political parties, the Crisis Staff was established. Sometime around the 19th of April, Miroslav Tadic joined the Crisis Staff - perhaps it was on the 20th of April - and he joined it as the commander of the TO staff [as interpreted]. And I think that we could take the 19th of April as the starting date for creation of the Crisis Staff, and it went on working until mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have just a second, because I have one document to possibly tender into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of my friends from the Prosecution, this is our internal number -- it's a page for Crisis Staff for the month of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see an error in translation, page 65, line 23. The witness said that Miroslav Tadic joined as the commander of the civil protection staff, whereas it says here that he joined as commander of the TO staff. So I would like that clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Miroslav Tadic, Dr. Simic, you meant to say that he was commander of civil protection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the benefit of my colleagues from the Prosecution, it's our -- well, internal number KS1. It's a payroll list for the month of May 1992. And maybe we could have some comments from the witness. Mr. Usher, please. This is the B/C/S version and English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we are wondering whether we could have clarification. What is the difference between civil protection and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ask the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Clarify with the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, can you please, if you know, explain the difference between the Territorial Defence and civil protection.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Both components are regulated by the law on National Defence. Territorial Defence is a military component that is armed and takes part in a war, whereas civilian protection consists mostly of retirees and veterans, disabled veterans who are involved in solving various issues within civilian protection, funerals, exhumation, protection of windows, and so on and so forth. Miroslav Tadic would be able to explain this in greater detail. All of this is regulated by the law on National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what is this document about.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a payroll list of the Crisis Staff for May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you said that at that gathering of Serbian assemblymen and in the presence of the members of the executive board of the SDS in that municipality there was some talk about creating Crisis Staff, do you see on this list the same people that were then at that occasion mentioned as possible members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That mostly corresponds to that, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I wonder if Mr. Pantelic would be interested in confirming whether or not this is an exhaustive and complete list of the Crisis Staff, because that would be of use to the Chamber, I submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's also my intention. But first let me correct the transcript. Page 67, line 18, I think it was not correct to say that that was the executive board of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me: The meeting in which Serb assemblymen participated, were members of the executive council of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac present as well?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't the executive board of the SDS that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And once you recollect what took place during that meeting, and if you compare that with this list, in April of 1992 when the Crisis Staff started functioning, can you tell us did it have more members than we can see listed here or what? Can you please give comment.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: While we had our consultations, more people were proposed as members. But later on, due to the war developments and so on, a number of people couldn't join the Crisis Staff. And by this I mean first and foremost Matan Asijovic [phoen] who was mobilised, then a possible candidate mentioned was also Ilija Ristic, who did not participate later on in the work of the Crisis Staff because he headed the veterinary service. And there were other people involved in similar circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And does this list in fact reflect the situation and the membership of the Crisis Staff in April of 1992, when according to you it started functioning?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who manufactured the stamp of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Administrative organs of the municipal assembly. Physically it was manufactured by Marko Kuresevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was between the 17th and 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into details, but if you remember what did that stamp look like? What text did it have?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In the middle it had four Cyrillic S's, and then it also had this text on it: "Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo Under Formation."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If we take a look at the English version of this document, we'll see that the copy is very bad. So could you please put your copy on the ELMO so that we can see what this stamp looked like.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It is not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But can you actually read what it says on that stamp.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It says here - at least the part that I can see - "the Executive Council."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic, page 69, line 11. I'm sure there must be something a little incorrect there, because there is no stamp on the English version. Just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right. As I said, there is no stamp on the English version, and my idea was just to check on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. No, I understand that, but at the moment it looks as though there's a stamp on the English version, and it isn't very clear, which doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. We shall take some steps to maybe ask the assistance of the interpreters' unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, why is there a stamp of the executive council here on the left side if this is a payroll list.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because the financial department was within the executive branch of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If there is no objection, I would like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have it numbered, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This will be marked Defence Exhibit 55/1, and that's for the English. And Defence Exhibit 55/1 ter for the B/C/S. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I make that clear though, on the basis that there is no concession by the Prosecution on authenticity at this stage, of course. I raised that point initially at the pre-Defence case conference the other day, and I'll reiterate that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I have just a little question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'd like to find out from Dr. Simic whether the payments in dinars, being that I don't know the value of the dinar in 1992, whether the payment for the month of May, whether this reflects a real salary of substance or whether it was more like an honorarium of some description. So to have a sense of how much and, as I've said, was it a real salary or some type of honorarium.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time the worth of this was very low. I don't think one could pay a drink in a coffee bar with this amount. And we had daily inflation of 10 per cent. We had a hyperinflation at the time, so this amount in dinars was practically without any worth. However, we did receive this payment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So what would, for example, the equivalent -- if you can recall. I mean, we've seen in the trial so far often times the equivalent has been put into Deutschmarks. If it's easier for you to maybe give us an equivalent in Deutschmarks or any -- any -- any sense for us, rather than simply to say that there was a high rate of inflation. I think we just need to get a sense of, shall we say, the financial worth of the job of being on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The republic government issued a decree in the Official Gazette which reflected that there was a daily inflation of 10 per cent. Financially there was no sense in doing this because the municipality had no funds, and it couldn't distribute salaries. No tax was levied. There was no budget. There was no financial assistance coming from outside either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, then, Dr. Simic, you and the other members of the Crisis Staff, including presumably Mr. Tadic, were not doing this for financial reasons but for political reasons -- in any event, you were almost volunteering your services. Is that the sense that I have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's the equivalent? Was it 300 Deutschmark? 150? Or 10 Deutschmark? Can you remember approximately what the equivalent would be?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: About 10 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, what about the salaries of other employees in other companies? Was it roughly at that level?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All of that can be seen from payrolls. Approximately everything is at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you mentioned Mr. Marko Kuresevic, who manufactured stamps. Do you know how many stamps contained the words: "the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo Under Formation," how many stamps of this kind were made?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I was informed - I did not take part in this; it's the administration that dealt with these matters - three stamps of this kind were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean with the same content?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The same content.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who used them? I mean, which institutions.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: One was at the Crisis Staff, and two were in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, could you explain to us: The decision to appoint you president of the Crisis Staff, how come it was dated the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They agreed at the Crisis Staff that this should be covered, this period of two days, and that the documents should be written from the 17th of April. That includes this decision to appoint me president. Actually, it was from the 19th of April, but it said the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean because of your years of service and things like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know why, but that's the agreement that was reached then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how were you elected president of the Crisis Staff? In which way? What did this look like?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The members of the Crisis Staff amongst themselves decided who their chairman would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you were practically voted president?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as a military reservist, according to the law on defence and the law on the army, you had your own war assignment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber whether "war assignment" means at any rate that you should have a military function or does that -- can that also imply some public offices and things like that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: War assignments applied to political positions -- to public positions and to military positions depending on what the Ministry of Defence decides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for work duty -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just for the purposes of clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- is the witness speaking about the situation prior to the creation of this Serb municipality, or is he speaking about the period of time well before, mid-April of 1992? I'm not sure which ministry he's referring to and which laws he's referring to and so on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the basis of what you know, was this principle applied in the former Yugoslavia in accordance with these laws and in Republika Srpska in accordance with these laws that were in force, those that had to do with war assignments?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, the concept of work duty, if one does not engage in active military service, if one does not go to the front line, to put it that way, do then civilians have some other options, to be in another position in accordance with the law on defence?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is that then work duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have some kind of work duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My work duty was member of the Crisis Staff, or rather, president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Dr. Simic, what about the members of your family? Did your wife have work obligation as well, your brother and the other members of your family that were mentioned earlier on this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My brother had military duty and work duty. That is to say, when he was off, he went to the front -- I mean, when he was not off he went to the front. And then he was here, he was on work duty. And my wife at that point in time, at the beginning of the war, was very pregnant and she had a baby on the 20th of June in 1992. That was her fourth delivery. My parents are very old, so they did not have military duty or work duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just two questions: How old were your parents then? And secondly: If your wife had not been pregnant, would she have been assigned a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Later already in 1993, she was assigned a work obligation and she worked at her own workplace, at the centre for social welfare. That is to say, when her maternity leave had expired. As for my parents, my father was born in 1925, and my mother in 1930, so at that time they were very old people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did your parents till their land? Were they engaged in agricultural activity?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They are always engaged in agricultural activity. But these are private activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this local environment in that village, did they give their contribution through their harvest and other things that they dealt with for the civilian population and for defence needs?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Like every household in a war situation, they helped by way of food. They gave what was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who required this from them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was the local staffs or the civilian authorities in the local communes, and they further organised help -- assistance to soldiers at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was this regulated by some regulations in a particular field?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This was regulated by various regulations. It was also left to one's own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have a document here which I would like to tender into evidence; it's a kind of certificate, our 36. It's a certificate issued by the Ministry of Defence, municipal department of the war assignment for Dr. Simic. I have the original also -- document here, as well as B/C/S and English translation. Ms. Registrar, we need only one copy for our records, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this document shows that it was issued by the Ministry of Defence, Department of Samac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I also see that your war assignment was head of the medical service in the TO staff in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on I see that your war assignment was at the position of vice-president of the Bosanski Samac Municipal Assembly in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you remained at that war assignment until the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From the 17th of April, 1992 onwards, you held the position of President of the Municipality of Samac and you remained with that war assignment until 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Assuming there is no objections from the Prosecution, I would like to tender that into evidence, please. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That will be Defence Exhibit 56/1 for the English and Defence Exhibit 56/1 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Usher, please. I have the original, too. It's the decision on work -- of assignment on work obligation, issued by Ministry of Defence, Samac department. I have also the original document to tender also. Since the B/C/S copy is not so legible, could we have the original, please, Mr. Usher, so that Dr. Simic can give us certain comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was issued by the Ministry of Defence, Municipality of Samac, Department of Samac. What's the date on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. And it says that you hold the position of President of the municipal assembly from which date?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please place that document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, I see in English translation that due to the bad copy, I would say, it was translated the date of 7 of April. But instead of 7, it should be 17. And you can -- you can -- you can see by yourself that number 1 in front of 7 is quite shade, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that's a correction, I mean, just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it should be 17th April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And I would like to tender this document into evidence too, if there is no objections. And please, Mr. Usher, could you please be so kind to provide this B/C/S version to our friend from the Prosecution just to take a look at this particular part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want it to clear with this document. The date on the left-hand top is 8th June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Correct. Because I believe that the person -- head of this department will come to testify here and he can maybe clarify why this document was issued on 1993 and he'll give details. So could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, this will be Defence Exhibit 57/1 for the English and Defence Exhibit 57/1 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to the period now of when the Crisis Staff began working, as you said. Where were you personally in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was -- in the evening hours, I was in Kruskovo Polje in my family home on the 16th, in the evening. And on the 17th in the morning, I was called to work in the outpatients department as a doctor in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who called you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was called up by the duty officer in the army, from the army, the military. And several other doctors were called as well; not only me. I was the only one that responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were several wounded persons whom I had to see to; I had to bandage their wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But before you go on with this line of questioning, I'd just like to ask Dr. Simic whether the person, Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who signed D57/1, is the same Bosko Ninkovic on Exhibit D55/1, number 11, in charge of information. So on the first exhibit, D55/1, he's a member of the Crisis Staff. And on the second exhibit, D57/1, he is now in the Ministry of Defence for Republika Srpska. I just want to know whether it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up this point. Was he a member or, rather, the head of the Ministry of Defence, the Samac department, Bozo Ninkovic I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After Milos Bogdanovic, the minister was Bozo Ninkovic, and he was head of the Ministry of Defence in the Samac department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the payroll dating back to May, he worked in the field of information. What did they do exactly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, he worked in the field of information, but he wasn't the head of the Defence Ministry because that was Milos Bogdanovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what did the field of information mean? What did this cover?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time we tried to come by as much information as possible, because we were in a media vacuum. We had no electricity. We received no newspapers. We weren't able to watch television. We listened to the radio very rarely. So somebody tried to -- so people tried to get as much information as possible to be able to tell the people what was going on in the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What party was he in?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Liberal party of Rasim Kadric [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you say Rasim Kadic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Rasim Kadic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: K-a-d-i-c, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And by nationality, I assume he's a Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could we have Exhibit P79.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me help you. Perhaps you're worried about whether I'm asking you whether you recognise the form of the document or the content, so let me say whether you've ever seen it. Do you recognise it by virtue of us form?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is he alone or with somebody else? Who worked on this document? Did he do so alone or with the assistance of others?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that the document was compiled under his control. Now, who actually helped him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you ever consulted yourself or in any way did you take part in the compiling of this document?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. You can take this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us briefly, please, or rather, give us a description of those first days. What were they like when the Crisis Staff began functioning? And this was, as you say, about the 20th of April, and it went up to the end of April. So what were the activities of the Crisis Staff? How were the decisions taken? How were the decisions prepared? What was the runner-up to the decisions, and what was your working day like in those few weeks?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I should like to describe the atmosphere that prevailed, which was an atmosphere of war. There were shells falling from all sides. We were under total encirclement with no electricity, no water. It was a very dark and dismal atmosphere, and even the sky looked dark under conditions of that kind. And in that general chaos and anarchy and everything that civil war brings with it - deaths, funeral, woundings and so on - we tried to introduce a certain measure of law and order or to establish some sort of civilian authority which would at least in the civilian sector introduce a little bit of law and order. The executive board did what it could. It was the first to take steps in that direction, and they tried to organise public kitchens. The Crisis Staff was in the process of being formed, and then it was looking for some premises to set up its headquarters. And the municipal premises, the upper floors of the building, were bullet-ridden and they were on the -- up at the front line itself. And we had to collect the necessary legal staff and create the necessary conditions for us to be able to function. So we started out from scratch. We had nothing to begin with, but little by little we were able to round up the people and to start resolving some of the problems that faced up. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I wonder if there could be a clarification in the transcript. The witness just referred to the Crisis Staff, and early activities, and said, "The municipal premises, the upper floors of the building were bullet-ridden." I wonder if we might get some more precision as to precisely which building he's talking about and its location and when they were there in that particular building. It's of some significance, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure, Mr. Pantelic, you'll get those details from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us first, please, where was the municipal building located?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We saw it here in some of the material we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Describe it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It is opposite the Territorial Defence building, right next to the Public Security Station building, and the Crisis Staff was never in that building. It was the municipal government that was housed there and the organs of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is the building on the banks of River Sava?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That building is on the banks of the River Sava and the lower floor is protected by an embankment, whereas the upper floor is exposed to the bullets coming from the Croatian side, so that they pierced the building, hit the building with their ammunition, that part of it, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was the first headquarters of the Crisis Staff located, physically speaking? Where were you? Where did you have your meetings in those first days?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, we would meet for several hours in those first few days in the building of the agricultural combine, the Poljara Privredna Binat [phoen], and then the Uniglas building, and then we went into some of the empty rooms of the municipal heating system plant. And that's where we were while we were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit D27/3 ter. This is -- I believe it's a map of Bosanski Samac. So maybe Dr. Simic can quickly point out the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed these positions at length, but let's see the diagram on the ELMO once again so that you can point out the different location where the Crisis Staff had its meetings. First show us peak -- perhaps it was towards the Sava River bank.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The municipal assembly building is over here for you to be able to orientate yourself better.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about Uniglas?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For a few days it was here, and then it moved to this area, to a commercial building where the municipal heating plant was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we started talking about how you made the decisions you took, what this process was like in the first few weeks up until the end of April, how the Crisis Staff worked until that time.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At all the meetings of the Crisis Staff, as this was a municipal parliament, we always had the president of the municipal government present and a representative of the Defence Ministry as well. All the decisions in the regular work of the municipal parliament and in these wartime conditions, extraordinary conditions, all the decisions are put forward by the executive council, the municipal authorities, or the president, if he is putting them forward himself, the president of the executive council. And the organs of administration prepare a decision and draft a decision in conformity with the law and then offer it up for adoption. If the voting, which can be secret ballot or public -- if the majority votes in favour - and we always wish to achieve a consensus - for a decision to go through, then the decision would be made public. It would be written, printed, and then brought to me to sign, and then sent out to the executive organs for them to check it out, to see that it is in conformity with the prevailing laws because the executive power had the responsibility of checking to see whether the decision was in conformity with the law. If not, it would be taken back to undergo the same procedure again. And if it didn't, that decision would be revoked and another one written in its place. That's what we did then and that's how we work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the professional side, who prepared the decisions? Who drafted the decisions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Every secretariat in the executive organs had professionals as members of the team. So every secretariat in every ministry has its professionals, well versed in their particular professional field. The draft is then sent on to the legal men to see whether they -- the decision is in compliance with the law, and then it is offered up to the municipal parliament. Once it reaches the municipal parliament, people of different professions, ranging from farmers to tradesmen, engineers, physicians, whatever, they are there to vote on the decision, whether they understand it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there so that we can move on a little faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but on page 85 and line 14, "printed and then brought to me to sign and then sent out to the executive organs for them to check it out, to see that it is in," and so on and so on. By saying so, do you mean that you had a personal responsibility for those decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't pass any decision personally. All of the decisions were passed by the institution. I, as a chairperson, as any other chairperson, only had to sign those decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But you told us that they were brought to you to sign and then sent out and so on. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said first that those decisions went through the municipal assembly first. They were debated there and so on. After the discussion, there would be a vote, either public or secret. If we had a majority, then a decision would be adopted and then technical organs, administrative organs, would type up the decision that had been adopted by the municipal assembly. And once they processed it, they would bring it to me to sign. And then after that, the decision would be sent out to executive organs because executive organs are one thing, administrative organs are quite another. And once they receive this decision and the executive branch is staffed by professionals only, by people who had been trained for that job by either the Ministry of Defence or Ministry of Agriculture or whatever. And then they would verify that decision once again to make sure it's in compliance with the law. And if it was, they would implement it. If they didn't think it was in compliance, they would send it back to go through the parliamentary procedure once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was your signature required?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody had to sign it. That was the procedure in place. Somebody had to sign decision in addition to the stamp in the legislative procedure, there also had to be a signature. This was regulated by the statute of the municipal assembly and the same -- it is regulated in the same way at the republican level when it comes to the republican parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now go down to our local level. So on behalf of the body that adopted the decision, you signed it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have a lawyer in your Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We had a lawyer in the Secretariat of the Municipal Assembly, or rather, in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have a lawyer in the Crisis Staff itself?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't know whether we had a lawyer in the Crisis Staff. However, administrative organs had to have a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What lawyer did you most often cooperate with?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: With Mitar Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was his task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, there. So if that was the case, Mr. Mitar Mitrovic, whose name I was trying to recall, is in fact listed as number 2, member of the Crisis Staff on the May 1992 payroll. I'm sorry. That isn't a question. I was just offering that bit of information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the only lawyer, qualified lawyer there and the secretary of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me, please: During those first few weeks, what did you personally do at the Crisis Staff? Please describe one of your days. I know that no days are the same, but briefly can you describe one of your typical days in terms of your professional and other responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The working day would start by first ensuring that we had all the necessary preconditions for the work of the Crisis Staff, and it wasn't easy to ensure that. After that, we would convene the session of the municipal assembly, and we would have to send out notices to people to attend sessions of the Crisis Staff on such and such date at such and such time. And it wasn't an easy task when there was no electricity for example telephone lines and so on. Later on, I would try to find Official Gazettes because the republican assembly at that time passed quite a number of decrees and other enactments. I think more than 300 of them were passed at the time. And we had to receive all that, analyse all that, read it, and so on. I, as a physician, had especially difficult time dealing with these legal documents. I had to read them and so on and to prepare myself as much as possible for meetings. Later on, we would have consultations with assemblymen of the municipal assembly; there were 50 of them. And each one of them insisted on being well informed and find out what various opinions were, and so on, and therefore president of municipal assembly had to inform various assemblymen on the situation on the ground and on the work of municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me please interrupt you for a second. MR. DI FAZIO: And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Before Mr. Pantelic proceeds to that question. I have certainly no objection to this evidence coming out. But to be of assistance to you, I think we should know what period of time the witness is speaking about. Particularly, as there's reference to a republican assembly and decrees being passed. Is this during the months and weeks immediately following April 17th? Do we have an up-and-running republican assembly at work passing laws and decrees? Something like that should be clear to the Chamber, I submit. He might -- the witness might be talking about 1993 or a later period of time. Is this during the Crisis Staff period, during the War Presidency period, when the municipal assembly got up and running again? That sort of matter should be made clear to the Chamber, I submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's my intention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
