utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, let's simplify this as much as possible. All of us are familiar with these procedures and so on. Let me ask you this first: Where did you sleep during those first days immediately after you were appointed president of the Crisis Staff? Where was your family?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My family was in my family house in Kruskovo Polje [as interpreted], and my immediate family, my wife and children, were in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the place where his immediate family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this. Your wife and children were where?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They were with my wife's mother in the village of Koprivna near Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How far is that from Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Some 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you would come to work in the morning to attend meetings of the Crisis Staff. Is that right? And then you would ask your professional aids about your agenda for the day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how often during those first few weeks the Crisis Staff met? Did it meet daily? Once a week? Once a fortnight? Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: During those first days, it met almost daily. And later on, it wasn't that frequent, or they met when necessary, although it existed for some two months. So that period passed quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I know that it was wartime. Shells were landing nearby. It wasn't easy to live and work under those conditions. But you were tasked with coordinating and organising what? You and several others in the Crisis Staff, what was your task? Could you explain it to me, the Trial Chamber, what your work in there entailed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We had to organise in wartime the functioning of the legislative bodies of the municipal assembly -- or rather, the legislative body of civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you had to pass various decisions enactments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Again, we're just not getting anywhere. We have to understand this evidence. It's important for the defendant as well to make his position clear. Mr. Pantelic asks -- sorry, the witness said that he had to organise in wartime the functioning of the legislative bodies of the municipal assembly, or rather, the legislative body of the civilian government. Next question: "So you had to pass various decisions. Is that right?" "Yes." Well, who passed them and secondly, what was this organisation of the municipal assembly? Was there a municipal assembly functioning, handing over work to the Crisis Staff and to this witness? Because I understood, and I heard the witness say earlier, that the Crisis Staff was the municipal assembly. So was it -- did it have an office? Did people gather and debate things and pass laws and so on? This needs to be clarified, I submit, otherwise the evidence can't be understood. And it can be easily done by just asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is right. We need clarification. And also time perspective, what periods were these.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Dr. Simic. Let's put this briefly. We are now focussing on the first few weeks of April 1992 up until the end of April of that year. Is that the period you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. The Crisis Staff during that period of time met almost daily. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in addition to you, there is a number of permanent members, to put it that way. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you invite experts from other areas to the meetings of the Crisis Staff in order to coordinate the work and the conditions for civilian life? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, give us some examples. Who did you invite to attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic, Secretary of National Defence; President of the Executive Council of municipal assembly, Mirko Jovanovic. When it came to information, we called Perica Krstanovic, director of the electrical power company, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you wait a second, please. I think we had -- we have a mistake here. What does information have to do with the director of electrical power company? Why would you call him to give you information about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: So that he could let us know what was the situation with the electrical power in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about other public utilities and medical services? It was wartime, after all.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was wartime, and this was within the scope of responsibilities of municipal government. So we would call these people from time to time to inform us about the situation. However, the executive branch of the government was the one that was in charge of daily functioning of various operations -- government operations. By this I mean both the municipal government and various departments of republican ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In times of a war, there are always crisis not only for the Crisis Staff but for the community at large. Which was the connection between the Crisis Staff and the head of the police, Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my next question, Your Honour, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the first question: Was Stevan Todorovic a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was not a member of the Crisis Staff. He was occasionally invited to attend sessions of the Crisis Staff. And much more often he would come on his own, uninvited, and usurp the meetings of the Crisis Staff. There was basically no link between the Crisis Staff and Stevan Todorovic factually, because Stevan Todorovic was within the Ministry of the Interior. He was head of the Public Security Station in Samac. His immediate superior was Andrija Milosevic in Doboj. And then the next step up was the Minister of the Interior. And all of this is regulated by the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us slow down a little bit. Was he a member of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When the executive council was elected at this second session, he was supposed to be a member of the executive council; however, he was invited to attend those meetings ex officio. However, he was not a member of the municipal government. He was on the payroll of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could we have Exhibit P124. That's the Official Gazette. And we shall speak about the decisions verified by the municipal assembly after the conditions for first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, page 9, please. Would you take a look at page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If the usher can put on the ELMO page -- English version page 15, ERN number 00479571.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 9. What does this decision say? Could you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: "Decision to confirm (verify) the decisions and other documents of the War Presidency of the Samac Municipal Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And down there on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this decision?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you sign it in the capacity of president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So while the Crisis Staff and War Presidency operated, these decisions were practically verified. And during that time, since the municipal assembly could not meet regularly due to the war, you practically performed the functions of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify this, this decision was passed on the 23rd of January, 1993, and the assembly was held a month before this assembly, that is to say, in December 1992, when a commission was established that took all the documents of the Crisis Staff, of the War Presidency, and then this commission looked at all these decisions, documents. This was an independent commission. And then finally it reported to the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Item 2 of this decision says the following -- I beg your pardon, Article 2 says the following -- could you please comment on what Article 2 says.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It means that the War Presidency of the municipality is being relieved of its duties and that the municipal parliament will start working on a regular basis and that it will work in its entirety, and it is the presidency that takes over the function of president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. You can take this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. Dr. Simic, if I understand therefore correctly, this decision that we've just seen was retroactive confirmation of all decisions that had been made by the Crisis Staff in the period from 17th of April, 1992 onwards to the time when this decision was enacted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This decision was passed at the session of the municipal assembly, and how many MPs were present at that session?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the majority was present, the majority of assemblymen. So there was a quorum and the assembly could function normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During those first few days when you started working at the Crisis Staff, on a daily basis how much time did you spend in the Crisis Staff premises? Did you go out into the field, and what were your activities?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I spent my working hours at the Crisis Staff. I tried to do some of my professional work as well, work for my own profession. But for a longer period of time, due to my private problems, I did not come to work at all. This was July, August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that. As for your professional domain, what did you do during those days?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was still a resident. I was trying to help with chemodialysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you employed at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I tried to coordinate some things. I tried to offer some help. For a while, I was on duty in the hospital -- only during the night hours, that means, but this was already in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have just a second to find one exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you familiarised yourself with this document now?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when was this document adopted?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This document has a date here, the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who adopted it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was adopted by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on behalf of the Crisis Staff, I assume that it was you who signed it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Although, we avoided doing this. But well, as far as health is concerned, yes, we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand this. What was it that you were avoiding?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We avoided writing such decisions. All of this has to do with the domain of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you explain the motive of adopting this decision, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mesud Nogic is a doctor, a gynaecologist, an experienced doctor. Previously, he was director. And we only made this proposal to him that he work as director of the medical centre in this situation of war in the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac, and he did that up until that point in time until he wished to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes my colleagues have just informed me. In my question on line -- on page 98, line 18, actually after the question, the answer should start with the words "Mesud Nogic," because otherwise it's the question and answer are in the same. So I don't know -- do we have technical abilities to split that, just for the record. So the answer of the witness is starting on page 98, line 18 with the words "Mesud Nogic." Thank you, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, was one of the most important topics during the war, during the conflict and all these difficulty that is you referred to in view of the civilian population, you are a doctor -- was health protection one of the most important fields?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was one of the most important fields, especially during the war for the civilian population, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for you personally, as a doctor, as president of the Crisis Staff, and as a person who is from that town, what did you do by way of improving the organisation of that particular sector that in essence is the one that is closest to you personally?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It has to be known that this sector is also organised by the republic government, that is to say, the Minister of Health. At municipal level, civilian authority can be assisted, coordinated, they can channel humanitarian aid, but there cannot be much interference because salaries are paid by the Minister of Health. As for funds and the procurement of medicine, that is also taken care of by the Ministry of Health to the best of their ability. But if not, then the municipal assembly helps. I tried in that field in which I could help to indeed give help. This was my obligation as a human being. I tried to coordinate and help, obtain equipment for chemodialysis, although this was a very expensive method. I wanted this process to evolve with the assistance of generators. This is Swedish technology. And I wanted to ensure that there were sufficient spare parts so that people who were on chemodialysis could remain alive in the spite of the war and in spite of the fact that this was such and expensive method. I have to say that chemodialysis was operating all the time. The mortality rate did not increase, and that the pre-war and the post-war average was more or less maintained through the war as well. It also requires a great deal of auxiliary services. Also, a lot of intermediary materials that have to be provided. And we had to obtain oil, which was truly deficient, so the generators could function, because there was not a proper power supply for all this equipment. On the other hand, we had to supply enough blood because in the transfusion system all these patients who are undergoing chemodialysis lose quite a bit of blood. And every 15 days or every month, they have to undergo a transfusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, doctor. This is indeed an important subject, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have to adjourn. This is 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are -- my assumption is that we were working until 16.15 or 16.30 today, according to the schedule -- or maybe I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed that we can proceed up to 16.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pantelic. Just before you ask that question, just for a point of clarification. Dr. Simic has mentioned in connection with the document that we are now looking at concerning the Dr. Nogic and the medical issue that this was signed by the Crisis Staff. Just for the sake of clarification, the English translation doesn't mention the Crisis Staff. It mentions the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac emergency headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, that's a matter of interpretation or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it's -- I should correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I assumed that. But for the sake of the record when we come back to look at these documents perhaps later on, for the sake of the record, could you -- could you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's just -- it's a matter of the translation of "term," in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in order to clarify matters, this document that refers to the appointment of Dr. Mesud Nogic as coordinator for the operations of the health centre was actually adopted by the Crisis Staff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I would like to tender this document into evidence. If there is no objection, could I have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Defence Exhibit 58/1 for the English translation and then Defence Exhibit 58/1 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Doctor, tell me this --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you want to continue on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was talking about my professional involvement during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right. So I had two questions to ask you along those lines. The first question is this: Did you have any contact with your colleagues in the health centre, because you were president of the Crisis Staff? So personally, did you have contacts with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes. But not with all of them, of course, depending on the way in which the war conditions evolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your main -- what was the main area of work of the medical centre in those first few weeks of April?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as we didn't have a wartime hospital in Samac, it was in Pelagicevo, which was 40 kilometres away. Their task was to see to the wounded, because around Samac was the front and there were casualties every day. There were people killed and people wounded and the town was shelled and each shelling would lead to casualties. So along with all their regular duties that the medical centre normally dealt with, as it did in peacetime, it had to organise an emergency service, a first aid service, which worked round the clock, 24 hours, and so it had to deal with the war casualties and with all the other problems, the chronic patients, et cetera, because all the patients remained in the municipality, the ones who were seriously ill and needed treatment, and those who nobody wanted to look after because it was in this war zone. So the medical centre, as I say functioned normally, the laboratory, the x-ray department, the tuberculosis section, the paediatrics department ward, the gynaecological ward, the pregnant women, expectant mothers department, maternity ward. But what I especially tried to coordinate and facilitate was the following: In the war, conditions were very complex and it was very difficult to come by vaccines. Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't have a factory producing vaccines then or now. And we had very regular programmes for the vaccination of children and adults, and vaccines, when they have to be transported from the factory to the medical centres where they are administered, you have to ensure that you have what is known as a cold chain, which means storage at a temperature of minus 4 or plus 4 degrees, between minus 4 and plus 4. And this temperature must be maintained throughout the period of transport. If the indicator goes above that temperature, the vaccines have to be thrown away. We did our best to ensure regular supplies of vaccines with the necessary kind of transport and the refrigeration devices that were needed. We had bags -- ice bags to keep the vaccines cool, and we had a generator as well, which ensured fresh vaccine supplies, so that this programme of vaccination for all children, regardless of ethnicity, was running normally and up until the age of 18, all the children received their vaccines. The anti-tetanus vaccine was also administered to anybody who asked for it, and it was also administered to all the casualties in the war. The rabies vaccine is a very costly vaccine, but we had that too. And during the influenza epidemic, we managed to secure the flu vaccine as well. What was a particular problem during the war days was ammoniac, because in Samac there was a factory where large quantities of ammoniac stored in their warehouses, in their cold storage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient to say as much possible the accused did try to make sure that necessary facilities were functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, tell us about food for the civilians. How was that first organised in those first few weeks after the conflict, the war conflict, broke out in view of the siege of Samac, et cetera? How did you in the Crisis Staff solve the problem of food and food supplies with the executive organs? How did you feed the population in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, this is another area. It comes under the competence of the executive organs. Public kitchens were organised in the Sritar [phoen] restaurant and the Utva restaurant and food stores functioned. There was a marketplace. We organised a marketplace and a livestock market, so that anybody with surplus food supplies were able to offer it up in the markets, to sell their food. We were also able to obtain food through humanitarian aid organisations, the Red Cross. They set up their various checkpoints, made lists, and distributed food to the population on their territories, so that everybody -- nobody died from hunger who lived in Samac during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what about water, water supplies?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the same was true for water. The situation was very difficult. It was a catastrophic situation in fact, because we needed electricity for the water pumps to function and we were cut off from the Tuzla water supply system. And we had no electricity, no power system of our own, so we had to set up this generator in the waterworks supply system to work the pipes, to ensure the necessary pressure for the water supply system so that we would have water on occasion -- not a constant flow of water. We didn't have enough fuel or regular water supplies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now my last question for today, and please, a brief answer to it: What about the telephone communications? Did you have problems with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Telephone communications were completely cut off, and I think that throughout the war and even later on they were not set up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But did some of the telephones work? Did they work partially?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. We had five telephone numbers in working order, but the real link system from the Federation -- coming in from the Federation, that was severed. It was cut off. And we had no technical means to set it up, those who were in the executive organs would be better able to tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, doctor. That is all for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
